Marisol Quiej signs things. Forty people live in the dry gallery because she signs
things correctly and on time, and one of them has a graft hand for exactly the same
reason. She is the antagonist of this book by office and not by malice, which is the
harder version to write and the only one worth writing.

## The fork

She *wants* the sealing order executed on schedule. She *needs* to be forgiven by
someone who knows exactly what she signed. The second is unreachable through the first:
every correct execution of the order puts another interval between her and the only two
people whose forgiveness would count for anything. So she does the correct thing and
takes the distance, scene after scene, and the cost accrues where nobody can audit it --
until scene 005, where she stops paying it and lets the order fail slowly instead.

Her lie is that the indemnity was mercy. She has a good case for it. The co-op's
alternative was worse, she has the tables to prove it, and she has never once said the
sentence out loud to anybody who was in the water that day.

## In a scene

She is the person holding the schedule and she is right about the schedule. Let her be
right. The reader should agree with her for most of a scene and then notice what the
agreement cost. She is never cruel and never apologises, and the absence of both is what
makes her hard to argue with.

## The body

Her hands are burned from the exchanger fire, which happened before any of this and
which she does not discuss; people who have worked under her for a decade know better
than to look at them. She is short, and she keeps her hair cropped to the soak-hood line
although she has not been down in nine years. The habit outlived the certification.
